data.text/html:
Sequence prediction with CPT and CPT+, explained by playing with it

An interactive companion to Philippe Fournier-Viger's video "The CPT+ Algorithm for Sequence Prediction".
Someone went to the gym (A), then a restaurant (B), then the movie theater (C). Where will they go next? You typed "hello how are". What is the next word?
Sequence prediction: given a set of training sequences of symbols, predict the next symbol of a new sequence. It is used for web-page prefetching, product recommendation, next-location and next-word prediction. Every method in this lesson follows the same two phases:
  1. Training: training sequences → build a sequence prediction model.
  2. Prediction: model + a new sequence (e.g. A B C) → the predicted next symbol (e.g. D).
We first build the classical models (DG, PPM, AKOM), see where they break, then build CPT (Compact Prediction Tree) by hand, query it, make it noise tolerant, compress it (CPT+) and finally race all of them on data.

data.text/markdown:
1 · Classical baselines: DG, PPM and AKOM

The video trains every baseline on the same two sequences: ||[S_1 = \langle A, B, C, A, C, D, D\rangle \qquad S_2 = \langle C, C, A, B, C, B, C, A\rangle||]
model what it stores how it predicts after context … x
DG (dependency graph), window ||(w||) arc ||(a\to b||) weighted by how often ||(b||) appears within the next ||(w||) symbols after ||(a||) ||(P(b\mid a)=\dfrac{\#(a\to b)}{\#a}||), using only the last symbol
PPM order 1 how often ||(b||) comes immediately after ||(a||) ||(P(b\mid a)=\dfrac{\#(ab)}{\#a}||)
PPM order 2 how often ||(c||) comes immediately after the pair ||(ab||) ||(P(c\mid ab)=\dfrac{\#(abc)}{\#ab}||)
AKOM (All-K-Order Markov) PPM of every order ||(1..K||) try order ||(K||); if the context was never seen, fall back to ||(K-1||), …, 1
The video's worked numbers: DG gives ||(P(C\mid A)=3/4||), PPM1 gives ||(P(B\mid A)=2/4||) and ||(P(C\mid A)=1/4||), and PPM2 gives ||(P(C\mid AB)=2/2||).

data.text/html:
DG, by hand for the last symbol A (it occurs 4 times):
  • P(B | A) = #(A→B) / #A = 2 / 4 = 0.50
  • P(C | A) = #(A→C) / #A = 3 / 4 = 0.75
  • P(D | A) = #(A→D) / #A = 1 / 4 = 0.25
Counting precisely with w = 2, A→B is found only 2 times (the B right after each AB); the slide in the video says 3. A→C = 3 matches the video exactly. Slide w to see arcs appear: a bigger window means more (and fuzzier) dependencies.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Training CPT: a tree, a lookup table and an inverted index

Every model above loses information: from a PPM or DG model you cannot recover the training sequences. CPT (Compact Prediction Tree, 2013) is lossless: it keeps all training data, stored compactly, in three structures:
  1. Prediction tree: each sequence is inserted as a branch from the root. Sequences that share a prefix share nodes (AB is stored once for ABC, AB and ABDC).
  2. Lookup table: one pointer per sequence, ||(S_x \to||) the node where it ends. Walking backwards to the root gives the sequence back.
  3. Inverted index: one bit-vector per symbol; bit ||((s, S_x)=1||) if symbol ||(s||) appears in ||(S_x||).
The video's training sequences are ABC, AB, ABDC, BC and BD. Step through the insertion below.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Predicting with CPT: intersect, look up, count

To predict what comes after a query such as AB:
  1. Intersect: AND the inverted-index bit-vectors of the query symbols: ||(A \wedge B = 11100||), so the sequences containing both A and B are ||(S_1, S_2, S_3||).
  2. Look up: follow each matching sequence's pointer and read it back from the tree.
  3. Consequent: take what comes after the point where all query symbols have appeared. The order inside the query does not matter, which makes CPT tolerant to order noise.
  4. Count table: count each symbol in the consequents. The prediction is the most frequent one.
The video's result: after AB the count table is C: 2, D: 1, so CPT predicts C. Build queries below by clicking symbols.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Noise reduction (recursive divider) and sequence splitting

A query can contain a symbol that never appears in the training data, or so many symbols that no training sequence contains all of them. Then the intersection is empty and CPT cannot predict. Removing the noise helps.
  • CPT, recursive divider: if the query fails, try every subquery with 1 symbol removed, then every subquery with 2 removed, and so on up to max level. For ABCD that means BCD, ACD, ABD and ABC, then CD, BD, BC, AD, AC and AB, …
  • CPT+, improved noise reduction: remove the least frequent symbols first. Rare symbols are the most likely to be noise, and far fewer subqueries are tried.
Coverage is the share of queries for which the model produces some prediction. Raising the max level pushes coverage towards 100%.

data.text/html: 11 subqueries tried. Symbol frequencies (number of sequences containing it): A=3, E=0, B=5, C=3

data.text/markdown:
5 · CPT+ compression: frequent subsequences and simple branches

CPT+ (PAKDD 2015) makes the tree smaller without changing its predictions:
  • Frequent Subsequence Compression (FSC): a subsequence that appears in many training sequences (here AB) is replaced by a single node ||(X = AB||).
  • Simple Branch Compression (SBC): a simple branch is a chain in which every node has exactly one child (e.g. B→C, or E→X→A in the video). The chain becomes one node (BC, EXA). Here a chain is only merged when the node above is not the end of a training sequence, so every lookup pointer still lands on a node.
Toggle the two compressions and compare the trees.

data.text/markdown:
6 · Experiment: race all models on synthetic route data

The paper races the models on real datasets (BMS, FIFA, Kosarak, SIGN, Bible). Here we use a seeded route model: each trip has a start segment (which identifies the route), then a shared corridor of ||(d-1||) hub stops, then a destination. The destination depends on what happened ||(d||) steps back, so a model has to look past the corridor to predict it. Noise inserts stray symbols (rare "typos" or common stops) and swaps neighbouring symbols. The two measures from the video, for each test sequence (predict its last symbol from the rest): ||[\text{accuracy}=\frac{\#\text{correct predictions}}{\#\text{test sequences}}\qquad \text{coverage}=\frac{\#\text{sequences with a prediction}}{\#\text{test sequences}}||]

Raw CPT is big too, but CPT+ compression shrinks it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

7 · Sandbox: bring your own sequences

One training sequence per line. Symbols are separated by spaces (gym restaurant cinema), or a line without spaces is read as single characters (ABDC).

8 · Quiz: predict, then reveal

Work each answer out on paper first. Q1 uses the video's ||(S_1, S_2||); Q2–Q3 use the CPT training set ABC, AB, ABDC, BC, BD.
Answered 0/5. Flip reveal answers when ready.

Recap

model lossless? noise tolerant? size prediction speed uses how much context
DG no a little (window) small very fast last symbol
PPM order k no no (strict order) small–medium very fast exactly k symbols, fails on unseen contexts
AKOM no no exponential in K fast up to K, with fallback
CPT yes yes (order-free matching, recursive divider) large but prefix-shared slower (bit-vector AND + counting) any prefix size
CPT+ yes yes (removes least-frequent symbols first) much smaller (FSC + SBC, splitting) slower than PPM any prefix size
Take-aways: CPT keeps all the training data (tree + lookup table + inverted index) and predicts by intersecting bit-vectors and counting consequents. CPT+ adds compression and smarter noise reduction. The trade-off is accuracy against speed and size, and the best model depends on the data: when the order really matters (e.g. words in the Bible), AKOM can still win.
